about: How Wi-Fi goes through walls. Factory #15, backlog row 16, playlist How tech works. One hard idea: Wi-Fi is radio waving about 2.4 billion times a second, and most building materials let it through (NIST, NISTIR 6055, 1997: 'the relative "transparency" of the majority of these materials'), but the loss grows with frequency ('Attenuation increases, generally, with increasing signal frequency'), so the higher 5 GHz band loses more (ASUS: 'effective transmission distance at the same power level is shorter than that of 2.4GHz'); metal blocks it worst and water soaks it up (Apple: water 'medium', metal 'very high interference potential'; FCC OET 56: RF at microwave frequencies 'efficiently transfers energy to water molecules', which is how household microwave ovens 'operate at a frequency of 2450 MHz (2.45 GHz)'). Wi-Fi's 2.4 GHz band is 2400-2483.5 MHz (47 CFR 15.247); ovens sit in the 2450 +/- 50 MHz ISM band (47 CFR 18.301): same band. Tip: center of the home, off the floor, in the open, not in a cabinet, away from the microwave (TP-Link FAQ 455, ASUS FAQ 1044838). Hero prop: the folded paper wave ribbon threading cut-paper wall samples; hero stamp SAME BAND on the microwave card on line 'twist'; screenshot hold = the floor plan on 'tip'. Narration-led: record the voice first and key every visual beat to its word times.

lines.text: To Wi-Fi, anyway. So how does Wi-Fi go through walls?
It's radio, waving about 2.4 billion times a second.
lines.say: It's radio, waving about two point four billion times a second.

lines.text: A government lab found most wall materials let the signal pass.
But the higher 5 GHz band loses more through walls.
lines.say: But the higher five gigahertz band loses more through walls.

lines.text: And water soaks it up, even a fish tank.
Here's the twist. Your microwave heats water at nearly that frequency.
So put your router central, off the floor, out in the open.
Is yours hiding in a cabinet? Yes or no.
